job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Karl Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts at 7:30 with a bus into the city. At Brightline Energy I'm in the billing team: customer disputes, wrong meter readings, standard replies, and a lot of Excel. I studied economics and passed, with no internships, and I got this graduate contract four months ago. I rent a room in a shared house in Southgate, and my dad, who drives a bus, calls on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because maybe now people stop panicking. At work, in the billing team at Brightline Energy, I'd tell Ayesha, who sits next to me, that the chatbot we trialled saves us maybe ten minutes a day. That's not a revolution. Online I'd mostly roll my eyes at the hype posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a relief and a small disappointment. I use an AI tool now and then to fix Excel formulas, and it's handy, but it hasn't changed my job. I like that my pay and my team stay the same while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on billing disputes, which is mostly calling customers about wrong meter readings. I'd take the Tuesday evening Excel and data course I've been eyeing at the college, 180 for ten weeks. I'd also keep paying 120 a month toward my loan and save about 100.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. I'm still a bit tight on money after rent, but nothing is scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your dad say when you told him about the chatbot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drives a bus, and he's in the transport union. He says the thing that matters is the boss treating you fairly, not the tools. I think that's mostly right, and I told him so over Sunday dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you notice first if hiring started to slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I would watch is whether Brightline starts cutting the graduate intake. We took four graduates last year and I've heard talk of three this year. A hiring freeze is a quiet way for things to change without anyone saying it.

say: I'd say the hype is **overdone**; the chatbot trial saves us about ten minutes a day.
I'd tell my team nothing big has **changed**.
think: I'm a bit **relieved**, because my pay and team stay the same while I learn.
I'd quietly watch whether Brightline **cuts** its graduate intake.
do: Take the Tuesday evening **data course**, 180 for ten weeks.
Keep paying **120 a month** on the loan and save about 100.
feel: I feel **settled**, though money is tight after rent.
S0.quote: A hiring freeze is a quiet way for things to change without anyone saying it.
fieldNote: Karl uses AI **now and then** and sees it as a handy tool, not a threat, in this world.
His real watch point is **hiring**: a quiet freeze on graduates would tell him more than any headline.

steps.text: Do the Tuesday evening data course at the college
Pay 120 a month toward the student loan
Keep handling billing disputes at Brightline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about this at work, properly, and soon. I'd ask my manager how the team's tasks will be split between people and software. Online I'd share anything that says workers should be consulted, and I'd probably argue with someone about regulation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, much of my day is exactly what the tools take first: checking meter data, writing standard replies, looking up accounts. I think the team of nine could be six in three years. I'm the newest, which isn't comforting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, properly, and become the person on the team who sets them up. I'd finish the data course and ask for a project that uses it. I'd also join the union branch at Brightline, which my dad has nagged me about for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of a knot, but there's something exciting in it too. I'd rather be in front of the change than behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would setting up the tools for your team look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I told Ayesha I'd help her write good prompts for customer replies, which would make me useful. People keep their jobs by being the one who knows how the machine fits in. I'm not saying that's safe, only better than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own savings or help from family would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My money gets tighter in a bad scenario. I have maybe two months saved, and my parents could lend about 500. If my hours were cut I'd drop the gym, stop the data course and move to a cheaper room in my shared house in Southgate.

say: I'd ask my manager how tasks will be **split** between people and software.
I'd argue online that workers should be **consulted**.
think: Checking meter data and standard replies are exactly what AI takes **first**.
The team of nine could be **six** in three years, and I'm the newest.
do: Use AI tools **properly** and become the person who sets them up for the team.
Finish the data course and ask for a **project** using it.
feel: I feel a **knot**, but also some excitement about being in front of the change.
S1.quote: People keep their jobs by being the one who knows how the machine fits in.
fieldNote: Karl moves **first** rather than waiting, which fits his steady, proven-first approach.
He is realistic about being the **newest** on a team of nine, and he accepts that being useful is better than waiting.

steps.text: Set up AI reply templates for the billing team
Finish the data course and ask for a data project
Move to a cheaper room in Southgate if hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the pace is the problem, not the technology. Two years leaves no time for training, rules or a plan. At work I'd push for a team meeting about what the company will do. Online I'd back calls for a public safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a billing job is gone in 18 months. Everything I do is language, numbers and rules. Brightline will keep a handful of senior people and a lot of software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending to the bone, saving 300 a month instead of 100, and give up the data course to keep cash. I'd join the union fully and go to every meeting. I'd also put my name down for an energy-sector apprenticeship, like grid technician, since hands-on work gets three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty scared, honestly. I feel angry too, because I only just started and I did everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call my dad that night and ask about his union's view. Then I'd text my friend Marcus, who studied electrical engineering, about a way into the trades. It's a strange feeling to start over at 22, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate telling your degree. What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three-year gap for robots is the only gap I can use. A cable job outside is safer than any desk by about 2031. I'd hate to say that to my degree, but I'd treat it as a real option, not a joke.

say: I'd say the **pace** is the problem; two years leaves no time for a plan.
I'd back a public **safety net** online and call a team meeting.
think: A billing job is **gone** in about 18 months, since it's all language, numbers and rules.
I did everything right and still feel I only **just started**.
do: Save **300 a month** instead of 100 and drop the data course.
Go to every **union** meeting at Brightline.
Apply for a **grid technician** apprenticeship, since hands-on work gets 3 more years.
feel: I'd be **scared** and a bit angry, since I did everything right.
S2.quote: A cable job outside is safer than any desk by about 2031.
fieldNote: Karl reads the **3-year robot gap** as his one usable gap and aims for a trade.
He is **scared** but practical, and he leans on his dad and a friend in the trades.

steps.text: Save 300 a month and drop the data course
Go to every Brightline union meeting
Apply to a grid technician apprenticeship
Ask Marcus how to get into electrical work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a chance if we act now. At work I'd ask what the plan is for retraining. Online I'd argue that governments need to fund training for people in desk jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I have maybe three more years in this job, and my degree isn't strong enough to protect me. I passed without internships, so my CV is thin. What I do have is time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the data course, then go for a part-time master's in data analytics, maybe starting year two. I'd use AI at work every day to build up proof of what I can do. I'd also save 200 a month and look for a team that builds the tools rather than uses them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the 2028 one, but there's pressure. Five years is long enough to try something, and short enough that I can't mess about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your parents for, and what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Sunil did a part-time master's while working, and he says it's miserable but doable. I'd rather suffer for two years than be stuck at 27. I'd tell my parents about it over a long dinner and ask for about 2,000 toward fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What changes with five years is that I can make mistakes. If the master's doesn't work I can switch to a trade at 24 and still have time. With two years I wouldn't have that room.

say: I'd ask at work what the plan is for **retraining** desk staff.
I'd argue governments should **fund** training for people in desk jobs.
think: I probably have about **three years** left in this job, and my CV is thin with no internships.
do: Finish the data course, then start a part-time **master's** in data analytics in year two.
Use AI at work **every day** to build proof of my skills.
Save **200 a month** and ask my parents for about 2,000 toward fees.
feel: It's calmer than 2028, but I feel **pressure** to use every year.
S3.quote: I'd rather suffer for two years than be stuck at 27.
fieldNote: Karl turns the warning into a **study plan** and a savings target.
He is honest that having no internships leaves his CV **thin**, so he plans to study.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in data analytics
Use AI tools at work every day to build a track record
Ask my parents for 2,000 toward fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and we should use it well. At work I'd probably keep my head down and keep learning. Online I'd say we need rules about who owns what these systems produce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine. I'm adaptable enough, and I'd have time to find a niche, perhaps energy data. I'd be 32, which is not old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Brightline for at least three years, get my data certificate and apply for an analyst role inside the company. I'd keep saving 150 a month and try to buy a small flat by 28. I'd also stay in the union and keep an eye on who's hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's the first one that feels like I have room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years makes people lazy. Is that a risk for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest I think ten years makes people lazy. I'd make myself act now anyway, because things can speed up. That would be my rule: act as if the short one were true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger friends starting a degree now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to younger friends that nobody can tell them what to study. What they can do is stay curious and build a bit of money. That's all anyone has.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** and we should use it well.
I'd say we need **rules** about who owns what these systems produce.
think: I think I'd be **fine**, because I'm adaptable and have time to find a niche.
do: Stay at Brightline three years and get a **data certificate**.
Apply for an **analyst role** inside the company.
Save **150 a month** toward a small flat by 28.
feel: I feel **fairly calm**, with room to breathe.
S4.quote: I'd make myself act now anyway, because things can speed up.
fieldNote: Karl sees ten years as a **runway** but forces himself to act early anyway.
He treats curiosity and a **little money** as the best protection.

steps.text: Get the data certificate while at Brightline
Apply for an internal analyst role
Save 150 a month toward a small flat
Stay in the union and watch for hiring news

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because there's no time to train and my CV is thin. What would help is a real public retraining offer, a notice period at work, and a chance to learn the tools on the job rather than being told to. A union deal would be a big part of that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that people my age get told to just adapt. Adapting costs money and time, and not everyone has a dad who lends 500. Someone should say that out loud.

headlineQuote: Adapting costs money and time, and not everyone has a dad who lends 500.
portrait: Karl is an economics graduate, four months into a billing job at an energy supplier, **renting** a room in Southgate.
He uses AI tools now and then and tends to move first once something is proven, rather than waiting.
His mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** as warning time shrinks, and each case becomes a plan.
He is progressive and blames the **pace** and weak rules, not the tools, and he leans on his bus-driver dad.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most: no time to retrain, a thin CV and a billing job built on language and rules.
whatWouldHelp: A real public **retraining** offer, notice at work, and learning the tools on the job with a union deal.
